name: Ingvar Kamprad
tagline: A dyslexic farm boy who built IKEA and preached thrift, simple rules and hard work.
startedFrom: He grew up on a farm in Småland, southern Sweden, a dyslexic boy from a poor family who found it hard to concentrate in school. As a child he sold matches from his bicycle, then fish, seeds and pencils. At 17, in 1943, he registered his own mail-order firm, IKEA, with money his father gave him.

definingMoment.text: From 1952 the Swedish furniture retailers' association threatened suppliers who sold to IKEA, and by the late 1950s IKEA could not get enough furniture. In 1960, having read that Poland's foreign trade minister would visit Stockholm, Kamprad wrote to him and was invited to Poland. In January 1961 he went to Warsaw with his father, his head of purchasing and a designer, and bought chairs, tables and fabrics; Polish prices turned out almost 50% below Swedish manufacturing costs. The boycott failed, and because IKEA could not buy what everyone else sold, it began designing its own furniture.

shadow.text: In 1942 he joined the Swedish fascist movement of Per Engdahl; he attended meetings, raised funds and recruited members, and in a 1950 letter to Engdahl said he was proud of his involvement. A 2011 book by the journalist Elisabeth Åsbrink reported that the security police opened a file on him in 1943 and, by opening his letters, found him recruiting for the Nazi party SSS; she also quoted him in 2010 still calling Engdahl a great human being. When Expressen exposed the links in 1994, he called them the most stupid mistake of his life. He lived in Switzerland from the late 1970s to avoid Swedish taxes, and IKEA's ownership through a Dutch foundation also served as a tax shelter. For years he said his influence over IKEA was limited; in 2011 Swedish television reported a Liechtenstein foundation, Interogo, set up in 1989, through which his family controlled Inter IKEA, and he confirmed it. Besides the old Volvo and the economy flights, reporters found, he had a villa over Lake Geneva, an estate in Sweden, vineyards in Provence and a Porsche. He made no secret of his alcoholism and said he kept it in check by drying out three times a year.

councilQuestion.text: What did you choose this week without first asking what it would cost you in money or time?

screen.notes: A real Swedish businessman (1926-2018), founder of IKEA, never a politician, campaigner or religious founder; no account of sexual contact with a minor or of sexual violence was found; he is in, and his dark side is his youth membership of Swedish fascist and Nazi movements (apologised for in 1994, but in 2010 he still praised the fascist leader Per Engdahl), tax-driven residence abroad and a tax-sheltering ownership structure, and alcoholism.

review.devilsAdvocate: I attacked each value against the Testament, the New York Times and AP obituaries, the IKEA Museum and three reports in The Local, including a 2011 one on his Liechtenstein foundation. Responsibility fell: he hid his fascist past until it was exposed and still praised Engdahl in 2010, and it rested on two sources. Humility, Hard work and Boldness held on three sources each. Simplicity was then dropped by the lead reviewer: the Times found his thrift partly an image (a Lake Geneva villa, vineyards, a Porsche), which a hostile reader could argue strongly against, and it now stands in the shadow; the blind pick's Ambition was added. All four quotes match the Testament or the Times word for word; three sentences were corrected and the foundation and the thrift-image facts were added to the shadow.
